newsitem.title: GERMANY: Europeans see French poll as risky gamble for euro.
newsitem.headline: Europeans see French poll as risky gamble for euro.

text.p: France's European partners see President Jacques Chirac's decision to call early parliamentary elections as a bold gamble that could make or break Europe's planned economic and monetary union (EMU).
Commentators on Tuesday were impressed by the boldness. They were less comfortable, though, with the risk Chirac had to take to prepare France for a single currency.
"Chirac's bold move commands a certain respect. It also demonstrates the weakness of French democracy as fashioned under General de Gaulle," the Daily Telegraph in London wrote.
"Doing something bad to avoid something worse," was the way Munich's Abendzeitung described Chirac's decision to call the vote for May 25 and June 1, 10 months ahead of schedule.
Although commentators assumed Chirac would win his bet and see his centre-right coalition returned, the setback for the euro that a defeat would bring loomed large in their analyses.

"A victory for the socialists and left-wing parties would mean a state legitimacy crisis could hardly be avoided and European policies, which are Chirac's priority, would then be seriously burdened," Germany's Die Welt said.
Alfredo Urrutia, chief economist at Societe Generale in Madrid, said a victory was not a foregone conclusion because French voters had proven fickle in the past.

"If it becomes clear that Chirac will make it, this will be good. He is key to EMU and a strong government ahead of EMU will be a good thing. But if Chirac fails to make it, it would be a very unfortunate loss at a very unfortunate time."
The image of the fickle French voter, seen in the Maastricht referendum in 1992 that former President Francois Mitterrand almost lost, popped up in comments in several other countries.
Piet Dankert, a Dutch Socialist deputy in the European Parliament, thought widespread popular opposition could block Chirac from launching the euro on time even if he wins.
Several newspapers noted Chirac's gamble came only a few weeks after the announcement by his main foreign ally, German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, that he would run for reelection.
"There's no doubt the two European leaders have decided to put their entire personal political capital on the success of the monetary union project," Rome's Il Messaggero said.

"Like Chancellor Kohl ... Chirac has decided the best defence is a good offense," commented the Sueddeutsche Zeitung in Munich. "Both have linked their fates with Europe and the transition to the single currency according to plan."

This made it even more difficult to hold up the project, it said. "When great men grandly commit themselves to an historic goal, there are no more excuses for a retreat. The monuments would get damaged in the process."

Bonn's General-Anzeiger sensed problems ahead if Chirac gets his majority because France and Germany differ over key issues like whether political or economic factors should be decisive in shaping the single currency.
"If Chirac wins, the French president will gain in stature in a decisive phase before the introduction of the common currency and the end phase of the reform of EU institutions.
"That could make him a difficult partner for Helmut Kohl because the Europe the French want is not the same as the less interventionist Europe that Germany would like to see."
North German Radio in Hamburg also saw possible rivalries between the two allies playing a part in Chirac's decision.

"To take part in the introduction of the euro as a fully-fledged leading power in Europe, and not just as a junior partner of the Germans, Chirac will do everything to fulfil the Maastricht criteria, even if this means pushing through an unpopular and draconian austerity programme," it commented.
Both the Guardian in London and the Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung noted the irony of a Gaullist president dissolving the National Assembly for the sake of European policy.
The Guardian suggested he might have done it "...to upstage Chancellor Kohl -- Europe, c'est moi."
